name: Hemp seed oil
lead: Hemp seed oil is a plant oil pressed from the seeds of low-THC varieties of Cannabis sativa. It is used as a food oil, in body-care products such as soaps, shampoos and moisturisers, and in industrial products such as paints and finishes.[1] It is rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids, chiefly linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid.[2][1]

In skincare and haircare, it is marketed as a moisturising, nourishing ingredient. The published research on it is mostly chemical and food-science analyses of the oil rather than trials of its effect on skin or hair; two small registered human studies of topical hemp oil products are listed, and neither has published results.[3][4]

For appearance, the draw is the oil's fatty-acid profile. Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are the fatty acids proponents point to when describing hemp oil as moisturising and nourishing for dry skin, and the oil is also eaten as a source of omega-6 and omega-3 fats, which is how it appears in bodybuilding and diet forums.[2][1][12] It has also appeared inside a chewable nutraceutical tested for UV-induced skin redness.[13]

Hemp seed oil is distinct from cannabidiol (CBD) extracts made from the flower and leaf. Seeds contain no cannabinoids themselves, but trace amounts can be carried onto the oil from plant material during processing, which is why analytical studies have measured cannabinoid content in commercial oils.[1][5][6]

paras: A phytochemical analysis of hemp seed oil found linoleic acid (about 55%), alpha-linolenic acid (about 16%) and oleic acid (about 11%) to be its most abundant fatty acids, along with a small unsaponifiable fraction.[2] Other descriptions also list gamma-linolenic and stearidonic acids in smaller amounts and an omega-6 to omega-3 ratio of roughly 3:1.[1]

Cold-pressed hemp seed oil has been reported to show antioxidant activity in laboratory assays, alongside other cold-pressed seed oils.[3] Formulation studies have examined how the oil behaves in emulsions of the kind used in cosmetic and pharmaceutical products.[8]

Hemp refers to non-intoxicating, low-THC cultivars of Cannabis sativa, distinct from high-THC marijuana cultivars that differ in chemical and genetic composition, production practices, product uses and regulatory status; hemp seed and hemp seed oil are described as having valuable nutritional characteristics.[14] Industrial hemp is grown for fibre and seed, and legalisation of hemp as an agricultural commodity and of hemp seed in foods is driving expansion of the food ingredients industry.[15] A 2026 review covers hemp use across fabrics, construction, food, cosmetics and medicine, noting growing recognition of hemp seed oil and protein in the food and beauty industries.[16]

Wikipedia describes the oil as produced in cold-pressed unrefined (green) and refined (clear) forms, with the refined type used mainly in body care and industrial products.[1] Ten industrial hemp cultivars approved in Canada have had their seed composition characterised, and cold-pressed hemp oil has been compared with flax and canola oils for physicochemical quality and oxidative stability.[17][18][19]

Refined hemp seed oil is used mainly in body-care products.[1] One US-listed topical product combining hemp seed oil is labelled as a tattoo-aftercare cream; its label describes it as relieving stinging, moisturising and supporting tattoo healing, and carries the warning 'for external use only'.[7] These are manufacturer label statements, not trial findings.

Hemp seed oil also appears orally in diet discussions. T Nation forum members list it among fat sources in meal plans and describe it as a source of essential fatty acids for diets such as the anabolic diet; one forum answer distinguishes hemp oil, from the seed and used in lotions and soap, from CBD oil, from the flower and leaves.[20][21][22]

Analytical studies of commercial hemp seed oils have detected cannabinoids, including cannabidiolic acid, in some products, and have developed methods to quantify them so that levels of psychoactive cannabinoids can be assessed.[5][6] Researchers describe the composition as varying with the cultivar and the manufacturing method.[6] Canadian and EU authorities set differing limits for THC in hemp food products.[1]

No published trial of topical hemp seed oil for skin or hair appearance was identified. A randomized, parallel, single-blind, placebo-controlled trial in healthy men aged 35 to 50 tested a chewable tablet blending hemp seed oil with banana-derived beta-carotene for UV-induced skin erythema, as a nutraceutical aimed at photoaging; the tablet is a combination product, so effects cannot be attributed to hemp oil alone.[13]

Other human studies concern joint and other health outcomes. A 2025 randomized double-blind trial examined topical hemp seed oil in knee osteoarthritis, a 2023 double-blind study tested hemp seed oil combined with beta-caryophyllene, myrcene and ginger extract in knee osteoarthritis, and trials of hemp seed with evening primrose oil have been done in multiple sclerosis.[23][24][25] A compilation of randomized evaluator-blinded studies in normal skin examined the tolerability of topical cannabidiol and palmitoylethanolamide, which are not hemp seed oil.[26]

Registered studies include an early-phase case series of a topical hemp oil rich in cannabidiol and varin for androgenetic alopecia (NCT04842383, planned n=40, status unknown),[4] a completed trial of hulled hemp seed and oil in overweight adults (NCT02400203, n=30), which concerned diet rather than appearance,[9] and a skincare study for acne, eczema and skin ageing that was withdrawn before enrolment (NCT05873933).[10] No results from these registrations were available.

card.summary: A fatty-acid-rich plant oil used in moisturisers and body care; the skin-specific evidence is thin.
card.aka: Hemp oil, Cannabis sativa seed oil
card.note: Not the same as CBD extract; no published trials of skin or hair benefit were found.

quick.overview:
Hemp seed oil is pressed from the seeds of low-THC hemp plants and is high in linoleic and alpha-linolenic fatty acids. It appears in moisturisers, soaps and haircare products.

Most of the published work describes its chemistry and quality. Registered human studies of topical use exist but no results were found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents attribute benefits to its essential fatty acids, which are described as moisturising and nourishing. This has been described mainly in product labelling and composition studies rather than skin trials.
quick.risks: Topical products carry standard 'external use only' labelling. Analytical studies have measured trace cannabinoids in some commercial oils. No clinical trial data on skin outcomes were identified.

chain: Oil supplies linoleic and alpha-linolenic fatty acids
Applied to skin as an emollient, or eaten as an omega-3 and omega-6 source
Softer, better-moisturised skin is the claim
angle.text: Hemp seed oil is used as a plant emollient in moisturisers, soaps and haircare, and eaten as a source of essential fats. Proponents link the fatty acids to nourished, less dry skin; direct trials of skin outcomes are limited.
